title: Year-End Money Checklist: 10 Things to Do by Dec 31
excerpt: A simple year-end financial checklist covering 10 money moves to make before December 31, from spending reviews to next-year planning.
quick_answer: A year-end financial checklist is a short list of money tasks to finish before December 31, like reviewing your spending, canceling unused subscriptions, checking savings goals, and planning next year's budget. Working through 10 quick items sets you up for a calmer, more confident January with no loose ends.
content:
As December winds down, a year-end financial checklist is one of the kindest things you can hand your future self, and it takes far less time than you'd guess. If the past year felt like you were just keeping the plates spinning, paying bills, covering surprises, never quite catching your breath, you're in good company. Most of us don't get a tidy moment to look back at our money until the very end, if at all. That's exactly why a quick December review pays off.

This isn't about grading yourself or feeling behind. It's a friendly sweep through 10 small tasks that close out the year cleanly and give January a running start. You can do most of them from your couch with your phone, in bits, over a few evenings with a cup of tea. Let's walk through what actually belongs on the list and why each one matters.

## Why Bother With a Year-End Money Review at All?

A year-end money review matters because it catches the small leaks and missed opportunities before they roll into another year unchecked. Forgotten subscriptions, unused gift cards, savings goals you drifted from, these quietly cost real money, often $50 to $200, and December is the natural moment to clean them up.

Think of it as closing the books on a chapter. When you take even 30 minutes to look back, you get three wins:

- Clarity: you see what you actually spent and earned, not what you assumed.
- Recovery: you find money that's slipping away and stop the bleed.
- A head start: January begins with a plan instead of a shrug.

The review also lowers money anxiety, because vague dread almost always feels worse than the real numbers. Once you've looked, you can act. And the tasks themselves are small, cancel one thing, check one balance, jot one goal. Nobody's asking you to overhaul your whole life in a week. You're just tidying up so next year starts lighter, and that feeling alone is worth the half hour.

## What Are the Top 10 Things to Do Before December 31?

The top 10 tasks are quick, concrete, and doable in an afternoon spread across a few evenings. Work through them in order and check each one off as you go. None require perfect finances, just a willingness to look.

1. Review this year's spending by category, using your bank's yearly summary.
2. Cancel or pause subscriptions you haven't used in 60 days.
3. Spend down or note any gift cards and store credits before they're lost.
4. Check your savings goals: how close did you get, and where's the money?
5. Tally any debt balances and interest rates on one page.
6. Use flexible spending account (FSA) dollars before they expire December 31.
7. Make any planned charitable donations for the tax year.
8. Update or set your beneficiaries on bank and retirement accounts.
9. Set next year's one big money goal with a number and date.
10. Draft a rough January budget so the new year starts funded.

Don't try to do all ten in one sitting. Two or three per evening across a week keeps it light and stops the whole thing from feeling like homework. Grab the free checklist below and tick off items as you finish them.

## How Do You Review This Year's Spending Without Getting Overwhelmed?

Review your spending by pulling one report, not scrolling twelve months of transactions by hand. Most banks and card apps offer a year-in-review or annual spending summary that sorts everything into categories automatically. Open it, and you'll see the whole picture in about ten minutes.

Here's how to make it painless:

- Find the yearly summary in your bank or card app, often under "insights" or "trends."
- Look at your top three spending categories first, that's where the real money went.
- Ask one question: which category surprised you most?
- Circle one or two you'd like to trim next year, don't try to fix everything.

Resist the urge to judge past-you. The goal is a calm look, not a courtroom. Maybe dining out hit $340 a month when you guessed $150, or subscriptions crept up to $95, that's normal and fixable. Seeing the pattern is what lets you set a realistic target. A [subscription audit](/blog/subscription-audit) is often the fastest place to reclaim $30 to $80 a month you didn't even miss.

## What Money Deadlines Actually Fall on December 31?

A few year-end money deadlines are real and time-sensitive, so knowing them keeps you from leaving cash on the table. Most personal-finance tasks can wait, but a handful genuinely expire when the calendar flips, and missing them means losing the money for good.

The deadlines worth circling:

1. **FSA balances**, which many plans forfeit after December 31, so spend that $200 on glasses, prescriptions, or supplies.
2. **Charitable donations**, which must be made by year-end to count for this tax year.
3. **Employer 401(k) contributions**, tied to your final paychecks of the year.
4. **Gift cards and store credits** with an expiration date printed on them.

Everything else, like your January budget or a subscription cleanup, is flexible and can happen in early January without penalty. Sort your list into "must do by Dec 31" and "nice to do soon," then knock out the true deadlines first. That way a busy holiday week never costs you real dollars. A five-minute triage now protects the handful of things that genuinely can't wait.

## How Do You Cancel Subscriptions You Forgot You Had?

Hidden subscriptions are the fastest money to reclaim, and most people are shocked by how many they're carrying. The average household pays for several streaming, app, and membership services they haven't opened in months, quietly leaking $30 to $80 a month. December is the moment to hunt them down.

Here's a five-minute sweep:

1. **Scan the last two bank and card statements** for anything recurring.
2. **Check your phone's app store subscriptions**, which hide auto-renewing apps you forgot.
3. **Look for annual charges**, the sneaky yearly $60 renewals that dodge monthly notice.
4. **Cancel anything unused for 60 days**, you can always resubscribe if you miss it.

Say you find a $15 streaming service, a $9 app, and a $40 annual membership you never use. That's roughly $30 a month, or $360 a year, back in your pocket. Cancel on the spot while you're looking, because "I'll do it later" is how these charges survive another twelve months. This is the single highest-value hour on the whole checklist.

## What Should You Do If This Year Didn't Go as Planned?

If your money year was messy, the year-end review matters more, not less, and it's not a report card. Maybe you dipped into savings for a car repair, carried a card balance longer than you wanted, or never hit that $2,000 goal. None of that means you failed. It means life happened, like it does for almost everyone.

Reframe the review as information, not judgment:

- **Name what threw you off**, a medical bill, a job change, an expensive month, so you can plan for it next year.
- **Find one thing that worked**, even a single month you stayed on budget, and build on it.
- **Set a smaller, realistic goal**, $1,000 instead of $5,000, so January starts with a target you'll actually hit.

A year where you learned your real spending is a year well spent, even if the balance didn't grow. Progress in money is rarely a straight line. What matters is that you're looking, adjusting, and starting the next year a little wiser.

## What Should You Set Up Now for a Strong January?

Set up your January budget and one clear goal now, while the year's spending is fresh in your mind. Ten minutes of planning in December saves you the scramble of starting from zero on January 1. You'll walk into the new year already knowing your plan.

Do these three things before the ball drops:

1. Draft next month's budget: list expected income, then assign it to bills, savings, and spending.
2. Pick one focus goal, save $1,000, pay off a card, get a month ahead, and write it down with a deadline.
3. Automate the first step: schedule a transfer or payment so momentum starts on its own.

Don't forget the holiday hangover trap: January often brings extra card balances and quieter income after gift season. Plan a slightly leaner month, maybe trimming $100 from dining out, so you're not caught off guard. If you tend to reset every January anyway, pairing this with a [monthly budget reset](/blog/monthly-budget-reset) routine turns a one-time cleanup into a habit you repeat all year. That's how a single tidy December becomes 12 calmer months, one small check-in at a time.
seo_title: Year-End Money Checklist: 10 Things to Do by Dec 31
seo_description: Use this year-end financial checklist to review spending, cancel unused subscriptions, and plan January. 10 quick money moves before December 31. Free printable.

faq_items.question: What's the most important task on a year-end money checklist?
faq_items.answer: Reviewing your spending by category is the biggest win, because it shows where your money actually went and reveals leaks like unused subscriptions. Once you see your top three categories, you can set a realistic goal and draft next year's budget. Everything else on the checklist flows from that honest look back.

faq_items.question: When should I start my year-end financial review?
faq_items.answer: Mid-December is ideal, giving you a few weeks to cancel subscriptions, spend down FSA dollars, and draft January's budget before deadlines hit. Don't wait until December 31, since some tasks like FSA spending and charitable donations must be done by year-end to count. A little lead time keeps it stress-free.

faq_items.question: Do I need to worry about taxes on my year-end checklist?
faq_items.answer: A few items help with taxes: making charitable donations by December 31, using FSA funds before they expire, and contributing to retirement accounts if you can. You don't need to file anything yet, just complete the moves that must happen within the tax year. Note them so tax season in spring is easier.

faq_items.question: How do I find money I forgot about at year-end?
faq_items.answer: Check for unused gift cards, store credits, cash-back rewards, and FSA balances that expire December 31. Also scan for subscriptions you haven't used in 60 days and cancel them. These small forgotten amounts often add up to $50 to $200 you can recover or redirect before the year closes.

faq_items.question: Should I make a January budget in December?
faq_items.answer: Yes, drafting January's budget in December means you start the new year funded and calm instead of scrambling. List expected income, assign it to bills, savings, and spending, and plan a slightly leaner month since holiday bills often land in January. Ten minutes now saves a stressful first week of the year.

faq_items.question: Which year-end tasks actually have a hard December 31 deadline?
faq_items.answer: FSA balances, charitable donations for the tax year, gift cards with printed expiration dates, and final 401(k) contributions tied to year-end paychecks all have real deadlines. Miss them and the money is usually gone. Everything else, like your January budget or subscription cleanup, can safely wait until early January without penalty.
